newsitem.title: UK: Fragile truce on EU ends on Conservative fringe.
newsitem.headline: Fragile truce on EU ends on Conservative fringe.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind managed to keep a lid on Conservative turmoil over Europe at the party conference on Wednesday but just hours later the argument erupted at a fringe meeting.

The European Movement, a staunchly pro-EU group, hosted a debate on Britain's place in Europe, but "Eurosceptic" party activists hijacked the meeting, packing the audience and jeering the main pro-Europe speaker.
Member of Parliament Quentin Davies faced rowdy barracking as he tried to put the case for Britain to keep its options open and not rule out signing up to a European single currency.

"The European Union is the right vehicle to ensure prosperity and security in the twenty-first century. Eurosceptics may have all the tactics for opposing that, but they have none of the strategies for the future," he said.
Arch Euro-sceptic MP Teddy Taylor was warmly welcomed when he argued that Britain would lose jobs and sovereignty if it moved further towards economic and monetary union (EMU).
"Our sovereignty is fading away. The EU already costs us a fortune and the price will be higher if we sign the suicide pact of EMU," he said.

The ruling Conservatives are split top to bottom over Europe and at this week's party conference party leaders have endeavoured to keep the topic off the official agenda, forcing delegates off to fringe meetings to let off steam.

Government policy remains that Britain will keep its options open and maintain a place at all the negotiations over monetary union. The government has pledged to hold a referendum if the cabinet decides it would be in Britain's interests to join.
But it has come under severe pressure from the right of the party to rule out the UK's entry into EMU in the first wave in 1999.
Right-wingers have hosted a string of debates and fringe meetings and will launch a new group, "Conservatives Against a Federal Europe", later on Wednesday.
Eurosceptic activists at Wednesday's meeting firmly believe that if the government took a harder line on Europe, it would not be trailing opposition Labour by 20 points in the polls.

"If we ruled out joining EMU we'll win the election hands down," said party activist Brian Rathbone after the meeting. "We can't go into the election saying we'll make up our minds in four months time. The voters won't buy it. The pressure is building on (premier) John Major to make the decision now."
